transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-15
Start: 16:30 PT
Duration: ~60 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jordan & Luca (Redwood SEs), Priya (Vectra Head of ML), Hannah (NLP Eng), Carlos (SRE), Tom (Procurement)

Auto-summary: Quick kickoff to align on POC success metrics for quality evaluation. Discussed golden prompts, regression suite, hallucination/format checks, scoring approach (automatic + human), workload sizing for benchmarks, timeline (4-week POC), and security gating. Action items and next steps captured.

Topics covered: POC success criteria; golden prompts and negative cases; regression tests and monitoring; hallucination detection and format enforcement; scoring rubric (automatic metrics + human review); throughput/latency sizing and bench plan; timeline and gating for Dedicated/VPC; security and procurement notes.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um, really appreciate you all making time. This is Maya from Redwood, AE on the account. We'll do a quick intro, outline goals for the poc and then Jordan will go deeper into the eval mechanics.
[00:22] Priya: hey Maya, thanks. Quick intros — I'm Priya, lead on the ML side, Hannah does the model work, Carlos takes care of infra, Tom's here to keep procurement wheels turning.
[00:40] Jordan: cool, hi all. Jordan, solutions engineer. Quick agenda: agree success criteria, collect golden prompts, cover regression tests and hallucination checks, and map a bench plan and timeline.
[00:55] Hannah: couple of ground rules from our side, we need very low hallucination rates for extracted entity tasks, and strict format enforcement — our downstream parsers break on stray punctuation.
[01:12] Maya: noted. Success criteria — can we walk through what would be a hard pass/fail for you? Priya?
[01:25] Priya: yeah; for us success is threefold: 1) precision on entity extraction >= 95% on our golden set, 2) hallucination incidents <= 0.5% as measured by our fact-checker, and 3) end-to-end latency P95 <= 220ms for our typical 128-token requests under 50 concurrent users during peak. If we hit those we can move to a pilot.
[01:48] Luca: good concrete targets. On hallucination measurement, do you use a human oracle or automated checks?
[01:56] Priya: we have an internal verifier for structured claims but we still do spot human checks — so combination.
[02:05] Jordan: perfect, that aligns with our typical eval. We'll propose both automated signals and a small human eval sample for calibration — maybe 500 checks.
[02:18] Tom: from procurement, contingent on SLA and data handling commitments. We also need SOC2 and a simple network diagram for VPC peering.
[02:32] Maya: we'll include SOC2 and the standard security packet, and Jordan will drop the VPC diagram.

--- Golden prompts discussion ---
[03:00] Jordan: so golden prompts — we recommend a set that covers nominal, edge and adversarial cases. For this POC we're asking for: 150 nominal prompts that reflect daily traffic, 50 edge cases (abbreviated inputs, long tails), and 50 adversarial/negative cases that historically trigger hallucination or format deviation.
[03:25] Hannah: can you give an example of the format you want for the golden prompts?
[03:30] Jordan: sure. Example nominal: "Extract customer name, email, and subscription tier from the following support transcript: <TRANSCRIPT>". Edge: "Given this abbreviated chat: <SHORT_TEXT>, output JSON with fields...". Negative/adversarial: inputs that contain conflicting information or quoted text to trip entity resolution. We'll provide a template in the spreadsheet.
[03:58] Priya: emphasis on exact JSON shape, missing fields must be null not omitted.
[04:06] Jordan: understood — we'll enforce schema checks in the regression runner. Note — sometimes transcription mishears K V cache as K V cash, sorry that happens in our docs too, so we'll validate both ways during tests.

--- Regression tests & scoring approach ---
[05:00] Jordan: our proposed scoring has two tiers: automated scoring and human spot checks. Automated scoring components: schema-validity (pass/fail), token-level similarity for text fields (embedding cosine or ROUGE/ROUGE-L), entity-level precision/recall, and hallucination flags via heuristics and external fact-check calls. We'll compute a composite quality score normalized 0-100.
[05:35] Priya: what's the weight split? We care most about entity precision.
[05:40] Jordan: propose weights: entity precision 50%, schema/format 20%, hallucination signal 20%, and fluency/semantic similarity 10%. We can tweak per your priorities.
[05:55] Hannah: for hallucination detection, do you have an off-the-shelf detector?
[06:00] Luca: we run a lightweight fact-checker that flags invented phone numbers/addresses and anchors claims against the repo when available; for structured extraction we compare against the gold labels. We treat flagged instances as candidates for human review.
[06:15] Priya: ok. We want a reproducible scoring notebook so legal can inspect the metric definitions.
[06:22] Maya: we'll hand over the scoring notebook and reproducible scripts as part of the delivery.

--- Workload sizing and benchmarks ---
[07:00] Jordan: now for load: Hannah, can you share typical tokens per request and concurrency?
[07:10] Hannah: typical request payload is ~110 tokens, sometimes up to 450 for full context. Peak concurrency expected is 50 concurrent requests, sustained during bursts up to 120 for short periods. Average QPS ~22, peak QPS ~80.
[07:32] Jordan: for benching we'll run: 1) microbench single-client latency profile for 128/512 tokens, 2) concurrency sweep (1-200 clients) to characterize P50/P95/P99, 3) synthetic replay of 10k representative prompts to measure stability and cost. We'll also run a longer 2-hour soak at 50 concurrent to surface caching behaviour.
[07:58] Carlos: on VPC peering, we only have a maintenance window after 10pm UTC, so scheduling matters. Also need IP allowlist details.
[08:10] Maya: we'll coordinate windows. Jordan will include a prescriptive checklist of firewall rules.

--- Benchmark success thresholds ---
[09:00] Jordan: baseline acceptance criteria for the bench: P95 latency <= 220ms at 50 concurrent for 128 tokens, error rate <0.5%, and no more than a 10% cost uplift compared to initial quote assuming quantized model. If those fail we iterate config — batching, kv cache modes, or a quantized variant.
[09:28] Priya: cost uplift clause is tricky; we need a clear cost model in the spreadsheet.
[09:33] Maya: we'll include cost breakdown per 1k tokens, per-hour instance, and an extrapolated monthly run-rate for projected traffic.

--- Timeline and gating ---
[10:00] Jordan: recommended timeline: week 0 kickoff (today), week 1 data collection + golden prompt submission, week 2 initial bench runs + automated eval, week 3 human spot checks + tuning, week 4 final report and pilot handoff decision. So roughly a 4-week POC.
[10:22] Priya: does that timeline assume Hosted or Dedicated/VPC?
[10:26] Jordan: Hosted is fastest — we can do the first bench in hosted within 48 hours of sample receipt. For Dedicated/VPC there is prep for networking and reserved capacity which adds ~1-2 weeks for peering and infra provisioning. We'll include both tracks in the plan.
[10:45] Carlos: note: our security team prefers VPC peering for any PII-ish throughput. We can scope a hosted data minimization run but the production pilot must be private.
[10:58] Maya: understood — we'll separate the bench plan into hosted quick-run and private deployment run.

--- Security and compliance ---
[11:30] Tom: procurement needs to know retention, encryption, KMS integration. Also any third-party subprocessors?
[11:38] Luca: we support customer-managed KMS for Private deployments and provide logs for audit. We'll send the subprocessors list in the security packet.
[11:46] Priya: can you confirm whether logs contain full prompt text in Dedicated?
[11:51] Jordan: for Dedicated and Private, customers control log retention and can opt out of storing prompts; hosted default keeps a short window for debugging but we can redact on request. We'll document these modes.

--- Objections & tradeoffs ---
[12:30] Hannah: one concern is format drift under long context; sometimes KV cache optimizations lead to clipped outputs. How do you ensure deterministic formatting?
[12:42] Luca: we have a schema enforcement layer post-generation that can correct trivial deviations and surface full failures for re-generation. That adds slight latency but reduces downstream parser failures. We can test both modes.
[12:58] Priya: also concerned about model regressions over time; what's the rollback story?
[13:05] Maya: our rollout tooling supports canary and automatic rollback on metric regressions. For POC we'll freeze model versioning and log all invocations to compare.

--- Recap & explicit next steps ---
[14:00] Maya: quick recap: Vectra success metrics (95% entity precision, <=0.5% hallucination, P95 <=220ms at 50 concurrent). Deliverables from Redwood: eval spreadsheet + golden prompt template, scoring notebook, security packet (SOC2 + subprocessors + VPC diagram), bench test plan and scripts. Customer deliverables: 200 sample prompts + 50 negatives, confirm VPC windows and firewall details. Timeline: aim for initial bench week of 2025-10-27, final report target week of 2025-11-17.
[14:40] Priya: that works. Please mark the final report week — we need a slide deck for our executives.
[14:47] Maya: will do.

[15:00] Tom: procurement question — what's the minimum contract length for Dedicated if we move to reserved capacity after POC?
[15:08] Maya: typically 3- and 12-month commits; Jordan will include a simple pricing sketch but doesn't bind the legal terms.
[15:16] Tom: thanks.

[15:40] Maya: ok, thanks everyone. Jordan and I will send the items this week. Anything else?
[15:48] Hannah: just please include long-context tests (450 tokens) in the bench.
[15:52] Jordan: noted, we'll include 128/450 token profiles.
[15:56] Maya: great. We'll follow up with calendar invites for the bench windows. Thanks all.
[16:00] (call ends)
